doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Current gigs at the Donnell Library and Greenwich Village
summary: Collier describes his steady Thursday gig, the closing of The Cajun, a new trio gig, and pros playing for their supper.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: You’ve managed to keep playing. Do you have a steady gig?

Yeah actually I’m very lucky. I have two steady gigs. Our band has been playing — with Dick Sherman’s band — at the Donnell Library which is over here on 53rd Street, a half a block from here. We’ve been playing there since 1976 every Thursday 12:30 ‘till 2:00 and off for the summers but we’ve been there all that time. And we have a nice crowd that comes it. It’s a beautiful little auditorium, one of the nicest auditoriums, small auditoriums in New York. The acoustics are marvelous. And they have a great big Steinway grand piano for us so we can always get piano players.
It’s like a lunchtime sort of concert?
It’s a concert. It’s a concert. It’s a jazz concert. People come in who are either on their lunch break or retired people who are looking for something to do. And then also we

were at The Cajun for 14 years which was a club, the last club in New York that featured classic jazz seven nights a week, and we also played there Wednesday at lunch. And they closed it down in August, they’re going to pull a building down. The place was making money and had good audiences, but they’re going to pull the building down and put up condos so that’s what happens. So I was able, luckily, to find another little restaurant in Greenwich Village called Greenwich Village Bistro and we can only — it’s a small room, we can only do a trio there. So I’m working with Pete Sokoloff who is our regular piano player with the Donnell Library band and with Peter Eckland, so we have this little trio. We are there on Wednesdays. So that still goes. And I feel I’m lucky. I’m in New York, I’m playing, I’m playing in New York twice a week. Hey, man.
That’s more than a lot of people can say.
It’s more than a lot of people are doing. And it’s getting worse and worse, there are more and more professional players who are willing now to play for their supper.

Literally play for their supper. If it’s a chance to play what they want to play — no interference, no requests, and if they can come in there and do that it keeps the chops up, keeps them playing jazz, and a lot of guys more and more are doing this. And that’s what you’re seeing. But I feel so great, I’m still playing.
